choices.text: Zinc is a transition metal, because any d-block element is one by definition
Zinc is a transition metal, because Zn2+ is coloured in solution
Zinc is not a transition metal, because Zn2+ has a full 3d subshell with no partially filled d orbitals
Zinc is not a transition metal, because it only forms compounds, never ions

questions.explanation: The trap claim is: Zinc is a transition metal because it sits in the d-block. The d-block label reads as the definition of a transition metal. Zinc(II) has a full 3d subshell: no partially filled d orbitals, so zinc is not a transition metal. A transition metal must form at least one stable ion with a partially filled d subshell, and Zn2+ is 3d10 - completely filled.
questions.misconception: Zinc is a transition metal because it sits in the d-block.
questions.prompt: A student is asked whether zinc is a transition metal. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Aluminium has one more electron shell than magnesium, so the electron is further away
Aluminium's outer electron is removed from a higher-energy 3p orbital, further from the nucleus and better shielded than magnesium's 3s electron
Aluminium has a smaller atomic radius, so its electrons repel each other more
The trend reverses after magnesium for all period 3 properties

questions.explanation: Both atoms have the same shells and aluminium has the greater nuclear charge, but the electron removed from aluminium comes from the 3p orbital: higher in energy than 3s and shielded by the filled 3s orbital, so it is lost more easily - the first dip in scene s3.
questions.prompt: The first ionisation energy falls from magnesium to aluminium across period 3, even though nuclear charge increases. Why?

questions.answer: Down group 2 each atom has more electron shells, so the atomic radius grows and the outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded. The attraction on the outer electrons weakens, so they are lost more easily to form M2+ ions, and reactivity rises down the group.
questions.explanation: Reactivity down group 2 tracks how easily the two outer electrons are lost: bigger atoms, more shielding, weaker nuclear attraction - the climb shown in scene s4.
questions.prompt: Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water, but barium reacts vigorously. Explain this trend down group 2 in terms of atomic structure.

questions.answer: Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine and iodine, so it displaces bromide (forming orange Br2) and iodide (forming brown I2). Iodine is the weakest oxidising agent of the three, so it cannot displace chloride. Oxidising power falls down group 17.
questions.explanation: Displacement follows oxidising power: down group 17 the atoms grow, an incoming electron is held less strongly, and oxidising power falls - chlorine above bromine above iodine, as in scene s5.
questions.prompt: Chlorine water is added to aqueous potassium bromide and the solution turns orange. Chlorine water added to aqueous potassium iodide turns brown, but iodine does not react with aqueous potassium chloride. Explain all three observations.

choices.text: Copper(II) sulfate contains more water molecules in solution than zinc sulfate
Cu2+ has a partially filled 3d subshell, so electrons absorb visible light in d-d transitions; Zn2+ is 3d10, so no d-d transitions are possible
Zinc sulfate is colourless because zinc is not a metal
The blue colour comes from the sulfate ion, which zinc neutralises

questions.explanation: Colour in transition-metal compounds comes from electrons moving between split, partially filled d-orbitals and absorbing visible light, as in scene s6. Zn2+ has a full 3d subshell, so there is no gap for a d-d transition and its compounds are colourless.
questions.prompt: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is blue, but aqueous zinc sulfate is colourless. What best explains the difference?
